title: Tradition or eclectic?
hookLine: you might deepen one tradition or keep drawing from many, tagged and apart; Ruth and Orpah both choose honestly (Ruth 1)
tomorrow: after Pascal died, a servant found something sewn into his coat. what?

lines: ONE FAITH, OR A LITTLE OF EACH?
ORPAH KISSES HER AND GOES BACK.
cards: Some friends grow up in one faith and go deeper. Some read everything and keep a little of each. Somebody always has an opinion about which is real.
The book of Ruth begins at that kind of crossroads. Naomi, an Israelite woman living in Moab, has lost her husband and both her sons.
She decides to go home to Bethlehem, and she tells her two Moabite daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers' houses. Orpah weeps, kisses her, and turns back. Ruth won't let go.

teach.h: THY PEOPLE SHALL BE MY PEOPLE.
teach.b: Ruth says: "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." So which daughter-in-law was right?
Look closely, and the book never blames Orpah. Naomi herself told her to go, and she goes back, the text says, to her people and her gods, with a kiss. Ruth goes deep.

She binds herself to one people and one God, and the book ends with her as great-grandmother of King David. Today's question: deepen one tradition, or keep drawing from many? This path's answer is that both can be honest.

teach.h: ONE DEEP WELL, OR MANY NAMED ONES.
teach.b: Ruth's way is a deep well, dug in one place.

teach.h: RUTH JOINS; THIS PATH JOINS NOTHING.
teach.b: The way this path has walked all along is the other: many wells, each with its name on it, never poured together.

What makes either honest is the same as in Ruth's story: you choose it with open eyes and love, not drift into it. Here's what this path shares with Judaism: a choice made with love and open eyes is honored.
Jewish tradition honors Ruth's, and reads her book at the festival of Shavuot. And here's the honest difference. In Jewish tradition, Ruth's choice is a full joining, one people and one covenant.
This path asks no one to join anything, and keeps each source whole instead.

how: Jews read the book of Ruth at Shavuot and honor Ruth as one who joined the Jewish people.

o: mixing every tradition together into one new belief
choosing whichever religion feels best on any given day
going deep in one tradition, or drawing from many kept whole

p: thy people shall be my people
when Ruth's book is read in synagogue

s: the book of Ruth condemns Orpah for going home
Naomi told her to go, and the text lets her leave with a kiss, unblamed.
Ruth, a Moabite, became great-grandmother of King David
the book ends with that family line.
drawing from many traditions means blending them into one
this path keeps each source whole and named, never poured together.

games.q: a coworker raised Baptist is going deeper into her own church; Zoe draws from many. is one of them doing it wrong?
o: neither: like Ruth's choice, each can be honest if chosen with open eyes.
the coworker is right: only one deep tradition is ever honest.
Zoe is right: sticking with one tradition is narrow-minded.
games.why: the book of Ruth honors Ruth's deep choice and never blames Orpah's return. this path ranks no one's road.

practice: Close your eyes and set two pictures side by side: one well dug deep in a single place, and a road past many wells, each with its own name. Don't decide anything.
Just notice which way you lean, the way a plant leans toward a window.

wordCard.voice: Tradition or eclectic: deepen one tradition, like Ruth, or keep drawing from many, tagged and apart. Both honest, if chosen with open eyes.

orig.note: Hebrew: Ruth, the Moabite whose choice to stay with Naomi gives the book its name.

carryVoice: Here's the line: my honest path, chosen with open eyes, the way Ruth chose. Day 1595, done.
